passage: I am Yamini, the neighbour upstairs. On Sunday I was on Rafiq's balcony, telling Rafiq's papa about the water tank repair, when Rafiq burst in: "Papa, Papa, a red bus, I saw a red bus!" Papa held up one finger and said, "Two minutes, dost, then it's your turn." Rafiq's mouth stayed open, feet danced on the tiles, and one hand pressed against the lips. When the tank story ended, Papa turned right away: "Now. The red bus?" Rafiq shouted the whole story in one breath.

qa.q: What did Rafiq say when bursting in?
qa.a: "Papa, Papa, a red bus, I saw a red bus!"

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling while waiting for the two minutes?
qa.a: Impatient and perhaps afraid the thought would vanish. The dancing feet and the hand pressed on the lips show a hard struggle to wait.

qa.q: What worked better than scolding in this scene?
qa.a: Papa's one raised finger and a promise of a turn in two minutes, followed by really giving that turn.

qa.q: What might Papa be feeling when holding up a finger instead of scolding?
qa.a: Patient and calm, wanting to respect the talk with Yamini and Rafiq's excitement at once.

grounding: A child interrupts an adult's conversation because the thought might vanish, and a signal plus a promised turn helps.

passage:
Monday: At school story time, Usha shouted, "My cat did that too!" in the middle of Ms Parveen's sentence, and again two lines later. Ms Parveen said, "Usha, please wait." Usha's shoulders dropped.
Wednesday: Ms Parveen knelt by Usha's chair. "When a thought pops up, put your hand flat on your chest. I will see it, and you get the next turn." They practised twice.
Friday: In a rainy-day story, Usha's hand went flat on the chest, cheeks puffed with waiting. Ms Parveen nodded, finished the page, and said, "Now, Usha, your cat?" Usha talked for a whole minute.

qa.q: What hand signal did Ms Parveen teach Usha?
qa.a: Putting a hand flat on the chest when a thought pops up.

qa.q: What might Usha have felt after hearing "please wait" on Monday?
qa.a: Discouraged, maybe a bit embarrassed. The dropped shoulders show the wish to share had been dampened.

qa.q: What turning point on Wednesday helped Usha wait?
qa.a: Ms Parveen knelt down, taught the hand-on-chest signal and promised the next turn, then practised it twice.

qa.q: What is it like for Ms Parveen on Friday to see Usha's hand on the chest?
qa.a: Encouraging. It shows the signal works and Usha is practising waiting, and Ms Parveen keeps the promise by finishing the page and then turning to Usha.

grounding: A child who blurts out learns to wait through a hand signal and a promised turn, over three days.

passage:
Kindergarten note, Thursday.
While I was talking with Gurpreet's mother at pickup, Avni (5) ran up and tugged my sleeve. "Ma'am! Ma'am! My tooth is wobbly! Look!" She did it three times. When I said, "Wait, Avni," her face crumpled and she said, "But I'll forget!"
I knelt and showed her a signal: put your hand on my arm, and I'll put mine on yours, which means "I know, your turn is next." She tried it. She held my arm, jiggling, for about a minute. Then I turned to her. "Now, tell me." She showed me the tooth, beaming.
I'll teach the hand signal to the whole class tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Avni want to show the teacher?
qa.a: Her wobbly tooth.

qa.q: Why did Avni keep interrupting?
qa.a: She was excited and worried she'd forget what she wanted to say if she waited.

qa.q: Why did the hand signal work better than just saying 'wait'?
qa.a: It promised Avni a turn and gave her something to do while waiting, so she didn't feel ignored or scolded.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's mother have felt during the interruptions?
qa.a: She was probably a little distracted but likely amused, seeing how excited Avni was.

grounding: Shows a child bursting into an adult's talk for fear of forgetting, and a hand signal that helps more than scolding.

passage: At the small shop in Kasauli, Papa was talking with Saurabh uncle about the price of apples. Sarika, five, pulled Papa's kurta. "Papa, I saw a monkey! A big one!" Papa kept talking. "Papa! PAPA! A MONKEY!" Saurabh uncle laughed. Papa didn't scold. He crouched and held out his little finger. "Hold my finger, Sarika. That means I know you're waiting. Your turn is next." Sarika held it tight, bouncing on her toes. Papa finished his sentence. Then he turned. "Now, tell me about the monkey." Sarika told him everything, arms wide.

qa.q: What was Papa talking about with Saurabh uncle?
qa.a: The price of apples.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when she pulled Papa's kurta?
qa.a: She was excited and bursting to share, worried the moment would pass.

qa.q: Why did Papa's finger-holding idea help?
qa.a: It showed Sarika she was noticed and promised her a turn, making the wait easier than scolding would.

qa.q: How might Saurabh uncle see the moment?
qa.a: He seemed amused, laughing at Sarika's excitement.

grounding: Shows a child interrupting adults because her thought might vanish, and a parent's signal and promise of a turn helping her wait.

passage: In a Seoul café, Soo-ah, five, sat beside her mother, who was talking to her friend Aiko. Soo-ah suddenly shouted, "Umma! The fish in the tank has a baby!" Her mother paused. "Soo-ah, I'm talking." Soo-ah's face fell. "But it'll swim away!" Aiko smiled. Her mother held up one finger and nodded at Soo-ah, then finished her sentence to Aiko. Then she turned fully. "Now show me the baby fish." Soo-ah grabbed her hand, pulling her to the tank, delighted.

qa.q: What did Soo-ah see in the tank?
qa.a: A fish with a baby.

qa.q: Why did Soo-ah's face fall?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and worried that the baby fish would swim away before she could share it.

qa.q: What helped Soo-ah wait better?
qa.a: Her mother's raised finger and nod promised a turn soon, which helped more than just telling her off.

qa.q: How might Aiko feel about the interruption?
qa.a: Aiko seemed amused and understanding, smiling at Soo-ah.

grounding: Shows a child interrupting because her discovery might vanish, and a parent's signal and promise of a turn helping her wait.

passage: In the kindergarten room, Manjula Ma'am was talking to Ira's mother at the door. "She's settling in well, and—" "MA'AM! I saw a snail with a GREEN shell!" Ira burst in, tugging at the sari. Manjula knelt down. She put Ira's hand on her own arm and squeezed once. "That squeeze means I know you're waiting. I'll finish, then it's your turn." Ira hopped and squeezed back three times. Twenty seconds later Manjula turned. "Now. A green snail?" Ira told everything in one breath. The next day she didn't shout. She just put her hand on Ma'am's arm.

qa.q: What did Ira see?
qa.a: She saw a snail with a green shell.

qa.q: Why did Ira burst in while Manjula Ma'am was talking?
qa.a: She was so excited about the snail that she was afraid the thought would vanish if she waited.

qa.q: Why did the arm squeeze work better than a scolding?
qa.a: It promised Ira a turn and gave her something to do while waiting, so she didn't have to hold the thought all alone 🙂

qa.q: What was it like for Ira's mother to watch this?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and impressed that the teacher handled the interruption kindly and taught Ira a new way to wait.

grounding: Shows a young child bursting into an adult's talk and a teacher's hand signal and promised turn helping her wait.
